thread.title_full: Midland's John Wilson named to USGA National Rules Committee - NewsBreak

author: Fred Kelly
title: Midland's John Wilson named to USGA National Rules Committee - NewsBreak
text:
By Fred Kelly ,
1 hours ago John Wilson (Courtesy of John Wilson) Midland’s John Wilson has spent a lifetime playing golf. Now, he has an opportunity to administer the game at the highest levels.
Wilson, 56, recently was named to the United States Golf Association (USGA) National Rules Committee, which means he now is qualified to referee any USGA open tournaments, including the U.S. Open, the U.S. Women’s Open, and the U.S. Amateur.
Wilson said that being a rules expert is right up his alley.
“I’ve been a golfer all my life, and I’m a retired lawyer. I like rules, and I like golf, and I like how they interact,” Wilson noted. “My brother-in-law is a teaching pro, and he and I got to talking about the rules of golf, and that’s what got me interested in it.”
Wilson’s first step toward becoming an official was attending a couple of rules schools in 2019, learning the ins and outs of the game, and then passing a demanding examination.
“Rules school is three full days from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. of book learning, and it’s intense,” he said. “The fourth day is for the exam, which you have up to four hours to complete. It’s akin to the Bar Exam. It’s tough. It’s 100 multiple-choice questions, and you can take it only once a year.”
According to Wilson, the 100-question exam requires 90 correct answers in order to pass and be considered an “expert.” He did better than that.
Wilson answered 97 of the 100 questions correctly, while also scoring a perfect 80 out of 80 on a separate exam.
Since becoming an accredited official, Wilson has administered dozens of Michigan PGA, Golf Association of Michigan (GAM), and Korn Ferry Tour (a developmental tour for U.S.-based pros who have not reached the PGA Tour) events throughout the nation. He also has officiated numerous high school events for the MHSAA.
“I would love to do a five-to-10-tournament run, whether it’s with the Korn Ferry Tour or the LPGA or the Epson Tour (an LPGA qualifying tour) or USGA tournaments,” he said. “But I’ll never give up doing Michigan events and high school events. I think it’s good to give back to the game that way.
“I don’t see it as a second career or a full-time gig, but I could see myself doing a lot of high-end USGA tournaments, for sure,” he added.
To be appointed to work the high-end events, Wilson will have to pay his dues at smaller events, which he is prepared to do.
“You have to get known and do a good job and work your way up to doing bigger tournaments,” he said. “ … Maybe in two or three years, I’ll be able to work a U.S. Women’s Open or a U.S. Amateur or a U.S. Women’s Amateur or a U.S. Senior Amateur.
“But you’ve got to prove you can do it,” he added. “I’m sure they (the USGA) watches and sees how you interact with the other staff and with the players and how you handle different situations. You’ve got to cut your teeth. You don’t come out in your first year and get to do the U.S. Open.”
Wilson said he recently was offered an opportunity to do some serious officiating – and traveling. After some consideration, he turned it down to stay closer to home.
“I had been in contact with the Korn Ferry Tour and the LPGA about possibly doing a five-to-10-tournament run, and they wanted me to apply for a full-time gig, but it’d be 26 weeks of traveling around the world,” he noted, adding with a chuckle, “I just retired (in 2023), and I like my wife, and I like playing golf. I just want to do select tournaments.”
Asked about the most challenging and interesting aspects of being a rules official, Wilson chuckled again while discussing the wild fluctuations between extensive down time and frenetic activity when a call has to be made or a dispute settled in a timely fashion.
“It’s two hours of boredom, sitting in your car, and then 10 minutes of terror when they call you in, and you’ve got to get (a rules interpretation) right,” he said. “That’s probably the most interesting and most scary part. The toughest part is trying to maintain the pace of play. That can really be a pain.
“At some tournaments, nobody will call you in, while, at other tournaments, you’re ping-ponging all over the course (making calls),” he added. “It can be stressful. You don’t want to be slowing the pace of play down too much, so you’re hustling all over and moving on to the next (situation). It can be stressful, for sure.”
A graduate of Alma High School, Alma College, and the University of Toledo College of Law, Wilson enjoys hunting, skiing, traveling, reading, and, of course, golfing in his spare time.
Incidentally, Wilson’s wife Amy and daughter Abby both won individual regional championships while attending Dow High.
Wilson’s best 18-hole round as a player is a 72, which he has shot twice – once at Torrey Pines in San Diego and once at Old Head in Ireland.
“Both days were just magical,” he recalled fondly, adding of Midland Country Club professional Jim Deiters, “Jim was with me during the first one at Torrey Pines. That was a good day.”
Wilson now will await his assignments for the 2026 USGA season, which he will receive in January. In the meantime, he will be officiating at the PGA of America Club Professional Winter Championship Series in Port St. Lucie, Fla., this winter.
“That’s a winter series specifically for club professionals, and Jim (Deiters) will be down there,” Wilson said. “It’s a pretty big deal, and I’m looking forward to it. It should be fun.”
